content: Peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase C (PPIC) is an enzyme encoded by the PPIC gene located on chromosome 5 in humans. This enzyme belongs to the peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase (PPIase) family and is responsible for catalyzing the cis-trans isomerization of proline imidic peptide bonds. This activity facilitates the proper folding and repair of proteins. Beyond its role in protein folding, PPIC is involved in several critical biological processes, including mitochondrial metabolism, apoptosis, redox regulation, and inflammation. It is also implicated in various pathological conditions, such as ischemic reperfusion injury, AIDS, and cancer. Structurally, PPIC shares similarities with other cyclophilins, forming a β-barrel structure with a hydrophobic core. This β-barrel consists of eight anti-parallel β-strands, which are capped by two α-helices at the top and bottom. The β-turns and loops within the strands contribute to the structural flexibility of the barrel. PPIC itself is composed of 212 amino acid residues and contains a hydrophobic sequence at its N-terminal that targets it to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). The PPIase domain of PPIC is homologous to that of PPIA and can be inhibited by the immunosuppressive drug cyclosporin A (CsA). The protein encoded by the PPIC gene is a member of the PPIase family, which catalyzes the cis-trans isomerization of proline imidic peptide bonds in oligopeptides, thereby accelerating protein folding. PPIases are highly conserved across eubacteria, eukaryotes, and some archaebacteria. The PPIase family is divided into three structurally distinct subfamilies: cyclophilins (CyPs), FK506-binding proteins (FKBPs), and parvulins (Pvns). As a cyclophilin, PPIC binds to CsA and can be found both intracellularly and secreted extracellularly. In eukaryotic cells, cyclophilins are ubiquitously distributed across various cell and tissue types, but PPIC is particularly highly expressed in the kidney. Cyclophilins, including PPIC, perform diverse functions beyond their PPIase activity, such as roles in mitochondrial metabolism, apoptosis, immune responses, inflammation, and cell growth and proliferation. PPIC, along with PPIB, is localized to the ER, where it plays a role in maintaining redox homeostasis. Depletion of these cyclophilins results in hyperoxidation within the ER. In the brain, PPIC forms a complex with cyclophilin C-associated protein (CyCAP), which activates microglia and macrophages through the calcineurin/NFAT signaling pathway. Clinically, PPIC, as a cyclophilin, binds to CsA to form a CsA-cyclophilin complex. This complex inhibits calcineurin, thereby blocking the signaling pathway required for T-cell activation. In cardiac myogenic cells, cyclophilins are activated in response to stressors such as heat shock and hypoxia-reoxygenation and form complexes with heat shock proteins. This suggests that cyclophilins may play a protective role in the heart during ischemia-reperfusion injury. Similarly, PPIC may provide neuroprotection by forming a complex with CyCAP, which activates survival pathways and reduces ischemic damage in the brain. Cyclophilin expression, including that of PPIC, is strongly associated with cancer pathogenesis, although the precise mechanisms remain unclear. For example, PPIC has been identified as a reliable marker for circulating tumor cells in epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC) and may serve as a biomarker for the detection and treatment of this malignancy. PPIC has been shown to interact with several molecules, including: Cyclosporin A (CsA), Cyclophilin C-associated protein (CyCAP), Calcineurin, and NFATc1.
